stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man born in Vietnam who moved to Australia at age 18. He is being worked up in your outpatient clinic for adalimumab therapy for severe Crohn's disease not responding to azathioprine. He is otherwise well and has no cough, weight loss, night sweats or contact with active tuberculosis in the last year. His BCG vaccination scar is visible on his left deltoid from childhood. He has no HIV and is not on other immunosuppressants.

Pre-treatment screening includes a chest radiograph reported as clear with no evidence of prior granulomatous disease. His QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) assay returns positive with TB1 antigen minus nil of 1.6 IU/mL and TB2 antigen minus nil of 1.9 IU/mL (positive cut-off 0.35 IU/mL or higher). Baseline sputum microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF are negative on three morning samples.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph clear; QFT-Plus TB1 1.6 IU/mL and TB2 1.9 IU/mL (positive cut-off 0.35 or higher); sputum microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF negative x 3; HIV negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step before starting adalimumab?

options.text: Proceed with adalimumab now because BCG history explains a false positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus result
options.rationale: Interferon-gamma release assays are not affected by prior BCG vaccination unlike tuberculin skin testing; a positive QFT-Plus indicates latent tuberculosis infection. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Commence rifampicin plus isoniazid plus pyrazinamide plus ethambutol for 6 months for active pulmonary tuberculosis
options.rationale: There is no evidence of active disease (asymptomatic, clear CXR, negative sputum); full RIPE regimen is not required. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay in 6 months and defer adalimumab until then to observe for indeterminate result
options.rationale: Repeat testing delays biologic therapy without adding information; a clearly positive QFT-Plus with negative active-disease workup is latent tuberculosis requiring treatment. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Perform tuberculin skin test to confirm latent tuberculosis before initiating any treatment given prior BCG vaccination
options.rationale: QFT-Plus is not falsely positive from BCG and the result is already diagnostic of latent tuberculosis; tuberculin skin testing would not add value. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Start isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 9 months for latent tuberculosis before adalimumab initiation
options.rationale: Standard LTBI treatment before TNF-alpha inhibitor is 9 months of isoniazid with pyridoxine; 3 months rifampicin/isoniazid is an alternative. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

explanation.summary: Screening for latent tuberculosis is required before starting biologic therapy or other significant immunosuppression, because reactivation carries high morbidity. Screening involves symptom review, chest radiograph and either tuberculin skin test or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA); IGRAs are preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals as they are not affected by prior vaccination. Positive screening with negative active-disease workup indicates latent tuberculosis. Standard treatment options are 9 months of isoniazid plus pyridoxine, 4 months of rifampicin, or 3-4 months of combined rifampicin plus isoniazid; biologic therapy can begin after at least 4 weeks of LTBI treatment.
key_points: IGRAs are unaffected by BCG vaccination unlike tuberculin skin testing.
Positive IGRA plus negative active-disease workup indicates latent tuberculosis.
Standard LTBI treatment: 9 months isoniazid plus pyridoxine.
Biologic can begin after at least 4 weeks of LTBI treatment.
explanation.pearls: Before TNF-alpha inhibitor start in a BCG-vaccinated patient, a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus with clear CXR is latent TB; treat with 9 months of isoniazid plus pyridoxine.

sources.label: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

stem:
You are the medical registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 74-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with a 24-hour history of confusion, poor oral intake and rigors. He was recently discharged after a 5-day admission for community-acquired pneumonia treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin. His usual medications are ramipril, metformin and rosuvastatin.

On arrival he is sleepy but rousable, with warm peripheries and a productive cough. Chest examination reveals crackles at the right base. Blood cultures have been taken and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g plus gentamicin 5 mg per kilogram have already been given within the first hour. He has received 30 mL per kilogram of intravenous crystalloid over the last 60 minutes. Despite this his blood pressure remains 82/48 mmHg, mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg, with ongoing tachycardia and rising serum lactate from 4.2 to 5.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, MAP 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 94 percent on 4 L nasal prong, temperature 39.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, warm peripheries, productive cough, right basal crackles, urine output 20 mL in the last hour
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) rising from 4.2 mmol/L; WCC 21 x10^9/L; CRP 340 mg/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 90 micromol/L); Hb 128 g/L; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion titrated to a target mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg or higher
options.rationale: Persistent hypotension and rising lactate after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid meet septic shock criteria; noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor targeting MAP 65 or above per the Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS guidance. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Give a further 30 mL per kilogram intravenous crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes before commencing vasopressor
options.rationale: Continued aggressive fluid loading after 30 mL/kg with persistent hypotension risks pulmonary oedema; vasopressor is the appropriate escalation. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Add intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg daily as continuous infusion for septic shock without vasopressor
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone in septic shock is used in refractory shock requiring ongoing vasopressor; it is not a first-line replacement for vasopressor. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Order urgent contrast computed tomography of chest to identify pulmonary embolism as alternative diagnosis
options.rationale: The clinical picture is septic shock from likely pneumonia; delaying vasopressor for imaging is inappropriate at this stage of resuscitation. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Commence adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram per kilogram per minute as first-line vasopressor for septic shock
options.rationale: Adrenaline is a second-line agent for septic shock; noradrenaline is first-line based on lower arrhythmogenicity. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

explanation.summary: The sepsis hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 mmol/L or higher, and start vasopressors during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP 65 mmHg or higher. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor, with vasopressin added second-line to reduce noradrenaline dose and adrenaline reserved for refractory shock. Hydrocortisone 200 mg daily is added for shock refractory to fluid and vasopressor. Source control and lactate clearance monitoring guide ongoing management.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if needed.
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor targeting MAP 65 mmHg or higher.
Vasopressin added second-line; adrenaline for refractory shock.
Hydrocortisone added for refractory shock on ongoing vasopressor.
explanation.pearls: In septic shock with persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg crystalloid, start noradrenaline first-line targeting mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg.

stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in the emergency department with 24 hours of left leg pain and redness. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin (last HbA1c 8.4 percent). He recalls no obvious skin breach but scraped the shin on a garden edge 3 days ago. The pain has become severe out of proportion to the skin appearance and he is now unable to weight bear.

On examination there is erythema extending from the shin proximally to mid-thigh with tenderness far beyond the erythema margins. The overlying skin has a dusky purple hue in the centre with early bullae. Crepitus is not palpable but there is marked oedema. He is diaphoretic and confused. Bloods show WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 380 mg/L (<10), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), glucose 18 mmol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (135-175). His LRINEC score is calculated at 9. Plain radiograph of the leg shows no gas in the tissues.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Erythema shin to mid-thigh with tenderness beyond margins; dusky purple hue with early bullae centrally; marked oedema; unable to weight bear
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 380 mg/L (<10); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88); glucose 18 mmol/L; Hb 128 g/L (135-175); LRINEC 9; plain radiograph no soft-tissue gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and reassess clinical progress in the next 24 hours
options.rationale: The clinical picture and LRINEC score of 6 or above are highly suggestive of necrotising fasciitis; standard cellulitis antibiotics alone would miss the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for exploration and debridement with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis requires urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin); mortality rises with every hour of delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the leg before deciding on antibiotic or surgical intervention
options.rationale: MRI is sensitive but requesting imaging must not delay surgical exploration in septic patients with a strong clinical picture; exploration is the definitive diagnostic step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Give a therapeutic dose of enoxaparin subcutaneously to cover the possibility of an occlusive vascular event
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is not indicated here and could complicate imminent surgical exploration for necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Discharge with oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily and mark the erythema for review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Discharge is unsafe in a septic patient with signs of necrotising infection; inpatient surgical and antibiotic management is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality of around 20-30 percent even with treatment. Discriminators from cellulitis include pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, dusky discolouration, bullae, subcutaneous crepitus (less than 40 percent of cases) and firm woody induration; absence of gas on plain radiograph does not exclude it. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) 6 or above suggests intermediate risk and 8 or above high risk. Management is urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin), with clindamycin included specifically to suppress exotoxin production.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, bullae, systemic toxicity suggest necrotising fasciitis.
LRINEC score of 6+ intermediate risk, 8+ high risk.
Absence of tissue gas does not exclude the diagnosis.
Urgent surgical debridement plus piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin, vancomycin.
explanation.pearls: In a septic patient with pain out of proportion, dusky skin and LRINEC 6 or above, arrange urgent surgical debridement with piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin; imaging must not delay theatre.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections
Australian eTG: Infectious Diseases - Necrotising skin infections

stem:
You are the general medical registrar in an endocrinology outpatient clinic reviewing a 46-year-old woman with 18 months of progressive central weight gain of 14 kg, easy bruising, proximal myopathy and new-onset hypertension. Her old photos show a rounder face and buffalo hump. She has type 2 diabetes newly diagnosed 6 months ago and now takes metformin 1 g twice daily. She has not been on any oral, topical or inhaled steroid.

On examination she has round facies, prominent supraclavicular fat pads, several purple striae on her abdomen and thighs greater than 1 cm wide, thin skin with easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness. She has no galactorrhoea, no visual field defect, and abdominal examination is otherwise unremarkable. She has never been on oral contraception. Recent bloods show HbA1c 8.9 percent, potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), and morning cortisol 720 nmol/L. She works day-shift and sleeps regularly. She does not drink alcohol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 164/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Round facies, supraclavicular fat pads, purple abdominal striae over 1 cm wide, proximal muscle weakness, no galactorrhoea, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.9 percent; potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); morning cortisol 720 nmol/L (140-620); no exogenous glucocorticoid exposure

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line screening test for Cushing syndrome in this patient?

options.text: 8 am plasma ACTH measurement to differentiate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
options.rationale: ACTH measurement is used AFTER Cushing syndrome is confirmed to establish the source; it is not a first-line screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: High-dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test as initial screen for ACTH-dependent disease
options.rationale: High-dose dexamethasone suppression is used AFTER confirmed Cushing syndrome to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH source, not for screening. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with 8 am cortisol measurement the following morning
options.rationale: The 1 mg overnight DST is one of three Endocrine Society first-line screening tests (with 24 h urinary free cortisol and late night salivary cortisol); failure to suppress below 50 nmol/L is positive. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Pituitary MRI with contrast to look for a corticotroph microadenoma as the primary diagnostic test
options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is used after confirming ACTH-dependent Cushing; up to 10 percent of the general population have incidental pituitary lesions, and imaging pre-diagnosis leads to false-positive workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: 24-hour urinary catecholamines and metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma before Cushing syndrome workup
options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma is a differential for episodic hypertension, not for Cushingoid features with muscle weakness and striae. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Endocrine Society recommends three first-line screening tests for Cushing syndrome, with two abnormal results required for diagnosis: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol under 50 nmol/L is a normal response), late-night salivary cortisol on two occasions, and 24-hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions. Exclude exogenous glucocorticoid use first. After biochemical confirmation, plasma ACTH determines whether the process is ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma commonest, followed by ectopic ACTH) or ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma, adrenal carcinoma). Further tests including high-dose dexamethasone, corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulation, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling then localise the source. Imaging is guided by biochemistry.
key_points: First-line screening: 1 mg overnight DST OR late-night salivary cortisol OR 24 h urinary free cortisol.
Two abnormal screening tests are required for diagnosis.
Plasma ACTH then distinguishes ACTH-dependent from independent disease.
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation, not before.
explanation.pearls: First-line Cushing syndrome screening uses the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (positive if morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L), the late-night salivary cortisol, or the 24-hour urinary free cortisol.

stem:
You are the on-call medical registrar. A 62-year-old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica on long-term prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 3 years is brought in by her husband with 24 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting and progressive lethargy. She stopped her prednisolone 3 days ago because she could not keep it down. She has no other medications. She has no known adrenal insufficiency diagnosis but has not had a Synacthen test.

On arrival she is drowsy and cool peripherally. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Her tongue is dry and eyeballs are sunken. Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 68). A random cortisol taken on arrival is 90 nmol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, HCO3 18 mmol/L, base excess minus 8, lactate 3.4 mmol/L. Blood pressure is not responding adequately to a 500 mL bolus of intravenous saline. ECG shows sinus tachycardia only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry tongue, sunken eyes, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); urea 12 mmol/L; creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 68); random cortisol 90 nmol/L; VBG pH 7.28, HCO3 18, base excess minus 8, lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram bolus alongside continued intravenous crystalloid resuscitation
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is oral only and its mineralocorticoid effect is not required acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone at 100 mg or higher provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: Withhold steroid until a formal short Synacthen test confirms adrenal insufficiency before administering hydrocortisone
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is life-threatening; treatment must not be delayed for diagnostic testing when clinical picture and low random cortisol strongly suggest crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: Restart oral prednisolone at 7.5 mg immediately and provide antiemetic to control ongoing vomiting
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone is unreliable in a vomiting, shocked patient and provides inadequate stress-dose steroid; parenteral hydrocortisone is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and start intravenous 5 percent glucose in saline resuscitation
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours plus intravenous glucose-saline for hypoglycaemia and hypovolaemia. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours as it does not interfere with a subsequent Synacthen test
options.rationale: Dexamethasone provides glucocorticoid effect but no mineralocorticoid activity; hydrocortisone is preferred in acute adrenal crisis for its dual effect at 100 mg dose. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is life-threatening and demands treatment before biochemical confirmation. Patients on long-term supraphysiological glucocorticoid therapy (prednisolone 7.5 mg or higher daily for 3 weeks) suppress the HPA axis and require stress-dose steroid during intercurrent illness. Standard treatment is hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours as 50 mg 6-hourly or continuous infusion, plus intravenous fluid resuscitation with saline and dextrose to correct hypovolaemia and hypoglycaemia. High-dose hydrocortisone provides adequate mineralocorticoid effect so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely; dexamethasone can be substituted only when a Synacthen test is planned within hours.
key_points: Long-term prednisolone 7.5 mg or more for 3+ weeks suppresses the HPA axis.
Treat adrenal crisis with 100 mg IV hydrocortisone before biochemical confirmation.
Follow with 200 mg over 24 hours plus glucose-saline resuscitation.
Fludrocortisone not needed acutely due to hydrocortisone's mineralocorticoid effect.
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis is treated with intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours plus glucose-saline resuscitation; do not wait for a Synacthen test.

subtopic_detail: Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man on the acute medical unit. He was admitted 3 days ago with severe hypokalaemia at 2.6 mmol/L and metabolic alkalosis after collapsing at home. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He has lost 8 kg over 3 months and reports increasing shortness of breath. He has no history of steroid use.

On examination he is thin with truncal wasting rather than obesity, and has hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa. There is no purple striae, no round facies, and no supraclavicular fat pads. He has proximal muscle weakness. Blood pressure remains 168/98 mmHg despite potassium replacement. Investigations show 24-hour urinary free cortisol 5 times upper limit of normal, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test cortisol 480 nmol/L (does not suppress under 50), and plasma ACTH 380 ng/L (10-50). High-dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows cortisol falling by only 20 percent from baseline. Chest radiograph shows a 3 cm right hilar mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Thin build with truncal wasting, hyperpigmented palmar creases and buccal mucosa, no purple striae, proximal muscle weakness
data_table.Investigations: 24 h urinary free cortisol 5x upper limit; 1 mg overnight DST cortisol 480 nmol/L (does not suppress below 50); ACTH 380 ng/L (10-50); high-dose 8 mg DST cortisol suppressed only 20 percent; K 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) after replacement; VBG pH 7.48, HCO3 32 mmol/L; CXR 3 cm right hilar mass

lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pituitary corticotroph microadenoma causing ACTH-dependent Cushing disease with paraneoplastic lung lesion
options.rationale: Cushing disease typically suppresses more than 50 percent on high-dose DST because the adenoma retains some feedback sensitivity; failure to suppress here argues against a pituitary source. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Primary adrenal cortisol-secreting adenoma with a coincidental incidental lung nodule from smoking
options.rationale: An adrenal source is ACTH-independent so ACTH would be suppressed, not elevated; the markedly elevated ACTH rules out adrenal adenoma. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Exogenous glucocorticoid use with factitious hypercortisolism and unrelated pulmonary carcinoma
options.rationale: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses endogenous ACTH; the very high ACTH here excludes this. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Cushing disease with rapid tumour growth explaining lack of high-dose suppression and mass effect on the lung
options.rationale: Pituitary adenomas do not metastasise to the lung; the picture, especially failure to suppress and speed of onset, is not consistent with Cushing disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma given the hypokalaemic alkalosis, hyperpigmentation and DST failure
options.rationale: Ectopic ACTH from SCLC classically presents with acute weight loss and truncal wasting (not obesity), profound hypokalaemic alkalosis, hyperpigmentation from very high ACTH and MSH, and failure to suppress on high-dose DST. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome causes: exogenous glucocorticoid (commonest overall), pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease, commonest endogenous), ectopic ACTH secretion (small cell lung cancer, carcinoid), and primary adrenal disease (adenoma, carcinoma, bilateral hyperplasia). ACTH is elevated in ACTH-dependent causes and suppressed in ACTH-independent causes. High-dose dexamethasone suppression test discriminates: Cushing disease usually suppresses cortisol by 50 percent or more (adenoma retains partial feedback), whereas ectopic ACTH does not suppress. Ectopic ACTH from SCLC classically presents rapidly with severe hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (very high cortisol overwhelms 11-beta-HSD2, causing mineralocorticoid effect), hyperpigmentation (very high ACTH cross-reacts with MSH receptors), truncal wasting rather than classic Cushingoid habitus (rapid onset, cachexia), and hyperglycaemia. Management is directed at the underlying tumour plus cortisol-blocking agents like ketoconazole or metyrapone.
key_points: Elevated ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome (pituitary or ectopic).
High-dose DST: Cushing disease suppresses >=50 percent; ectopic ACTH does not.
Ectopic ACTH from SCLC causes rapid onset, hypokalaemic alkalosis, hyperpigmentation.
Truncal wasting rather than classic Cushingoid habitus is typical of ectopic ACTH.
explanation.pearls: In hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with hyperpigmentation, failure to suppress on high-dose dexamethasone and a lung mass in a smoker, suspect ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma.
